10.1002_adfm.202517245: Silicon (Si) anodes, while theoretically surpassing graphite in capacity, face commercialization challenges from inherent volume fluctuations (>300%) and costly nano‐engineering processes. This study presents a sustainable solution through photovoltaic silicon waste upcycling into structurally optimized silicon/carbon (Si/C) nanofibers with Nb 2 O 5 ‐mediated interfacial chemistry. The designed architecture features a 3D continuous carbon network enabling efficient stress redistribution during lithiation and Nb 2 O 5 quantum dots embedding within the outer layer that dual‐functionalizes as both hydrogen fluoride (HF) corrosion inhibitor and Li⁺ diffusion promoter. Electrochemical characterization reveals stabilized solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) due to the robust 3D network and suppress HF attack by Nb 2 O 5 quantum dots. Benefiting from the enhanced structural stability and interfacial compatibility, the resultant Nb 2 O 5 ‐engineered Si/C anode achieves 77.3% initial Coulombic efficiency with 780 mAh g −1 retention after 1000 cycles at 1.0 A g −1 (0.023% capacity decay per cycle), outperforming state‐of‐the‐art recycled Si anodes in both cyclability and cost‐effectiveness. This study pioneers a dual‐approach strategy that simultaneously establishes a sustainable upstream silicon source through photovoltaic waste valorization and resolves the persistent challenges of cyclic volumetric expansion and interfacial instability inherent to silicon anodes.
10.1002_anie.202520653: Wet‐chemical processing of metals, for example, galvanic deposition, etching, and nanoparticle synthesis, usually requires complexing agents. In particular, for noble metal processing, anionic complexing species, such as halides or sulfide are indispensable. While it is known that these species strongly adsorb on metal surfaces and affect metal nucleation and growth, the detailed role of these anions in the underlying atomistic processes is less clear. Often, it is assumed that surface complexes are involved, but experimental evidence for the latter is still lacking. Here, we present direct in situ video‐rate scanning tunneling microscopy observations of gold–bromide and gold–sulfur surface complexes on Au(100) electrodes. Based on the intramolecular resolution images obtained in these studies, these species can be assigned to a dimeric planar and a linear complex. Once formed, the surfaces complexes are stable even at rather negative potentials and diffuse as molecular species on the Au surface.
10.1002_cssc.70933: The Cover Feature illustrates a solar-driven circular economy approach, in which plastic waste valorization is coupled with hydrogen production. A Ni/SiOx/n-Si photoanode promotes oxidation reactions under sunlight, while water reduction occurs at the cathode. This integrated photoelectrochemical system highlights a sustainable route for converting plastic waste and solar energy into valuable chemical products. More information can be found in the Research Article by B. Fabre and co-workers (DOI: 10.1002/cssc.70852).
10.1021_acsenergylett.5c03514: Perovskite oxides are promising solid oxide cell electrodes, yet their long-term stability is limited by performance degradation driven by cation segregation at operating temperatures. Conventional doping strategies to mitigate segregation compromise bulk transport properties or surface reaction kinetics by reducing oxygen-vacancy concentrations, representing an inherent trade-off between stability and activity. Here, a surface-specific strategy reconciles this dilemma by depositing an oxygen-deficient ZrO x nanocoating via atomic layer deposition (ALD) on Sr 2 Fe 1.5 Mo 0.5 O 6−δ (SFMO) electrodes. This vacancy-rich ZrO x coating achieves dual-function simultaneously: (1) a high concentration of oxygen vacancies drives Sr 2+ ions inward, while (2) self-forming Zr–O–Fe interlayers stabilize elastic and electrostatic force, effectively suppressing surface Sr accumulation. Furthermore, high oxygen deficiency maintains fast oxygen reaction kinetics. This nanocoating stabilizes SFMO electrodes at 800 °C for 50 h with minimal performance degradation, retaining the unsegregated SFMO electrode activity. This strategy provides generalizable routes for stabilizing perovskite oxide devices in high-temperature environments.
